summary: Defines the core schema for SCIM, the common set of attributes and resource types for things such as users and groups. The goal is to make user management in cloud applications simpler and cheaper by giving everyone a shared way to describe identities.

eli5.summary: This is a shared form with the same boxes for name, email and group, so every system describes people the same way.

subtitle: A shared JSON vocabulary for describing users, groups and other identities so that systems stop inventing their own.

tldr.problem: Cloud services each manage users in their own non-standard way, so organizations that use several providers must write redundant integration code for every one.
tldr.mechanism: SCIM defines a JSON schema and extension model: a few core resource types (User, Group), a set of common attributes, per-attribute characteristics such as mutability, and discovery resources that let a server describe its own schema.
tldr.outcome: Clients and service providers can describe identities in the same way and extend the schema without clashes. RFC 7643 has since been updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967.

facts.label: Data types
facts.value: 8 (string, boolean, decimal, integer, dateTime, binary, reference, complex)

today: RFC 7643 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2015. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967, so read those together with it. It is the schema half of SCIM; the HTTP protocol is in RFC 7644.

sections.title: Why a Common Identity Schema
sections.content:
Existing standards for describing and exchanging user information can be hard to implement. Their wire protocols do not easily traverse firewalls and are not easily layered onto web protocols. As a result, many cloud providers built non-standard protocols for managing users, which raises the cost of adopting products from several providers because each needs its own integration work.

SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) answers this with a specification suite. This document, RFC 7643, is the core schema: a JSON-based schema and extension model for users, groups and service provider configuration. Its companion, RFC 7644, defines the HTTP protocol that carries these resources.

The design drew on earlier work including PortableContacts, vCards (RFC 6350) and LDAP directory services (RFC 4512). Two roles recur throughout: the client (the application that manages identity data) and the service provider (the HTTP application that holds it).
sections.eli5: Many websites keep lists of people, and each one wrote the list in its own secret way. SCIM gives them all one common way to write the list so they can share it.

sections.title: Attributes and Data Types
sections.content:
SCIM schema is attribute based, not document based like XML Schema. Each attribute has its own type, mutability, cardinality and returnability, and the receiver validates documents in the context of a request. Attribute names are case insensitive, usually camel-cased, start with a letter and may then contain letters, digits, dollar signs, hyphens and underscores.

There are eight data types, all mapped onto JSON: string, boolean, decimal, integer, dateTime, binary, reference and complex. A complex attribute is built from simple sub-attributes and MUST NOT contain sub-attributes that are themselves complex. A reference is a URI, and by convention is carried in a $ref sub-attribute.

Multi-valued attributes are JSON arrays. Unless defined otherwise, their elements can carry the sub-attributes type (a label such as work or home), primary (a boolean that may be true at most once), display, value and $ref. Servers SHOULD NOT return the same (type, value) pair twice. Unassigned attributes, null and empty arrays are all equivalent in state.
sections.eli5: Every box on the form says what kind of answer it wants: a word, yes or no, a number, a date or a link. A box can also hold a small list, like several phone numbers where one is marked as the favorite.

sections.title: Resources, Common Attributes and Extensions
sections.content:
Every SCIM resource is a JSON object with a resource type, a REQUIRED schemas array of URIs naming the schemas in use, and attributes. Three kinds of attribute appear: common attributes that every resource has, core attributes defined by the resource type's base schema, and extended attributes.

The common attributes are id, externalId and meta. The id is issued by the service provider, MUST be stable and non-reassignable, and MUST NOT be specified by the client. The string bulkId is reserved and cannot appear in an id. The externalId is issued by the provisioning client so it can find a resource using its own identifier. The meta attribute is set by the server and holds resourceType, created, lastModified, location and version. The version must match the HTTP ETag, and is marked weak with a W/ prefix when the entity-tag is not a strong validator.

Extensions are additive, like LDAP auxiliary object classes, with no inheritance. Each extension's attributes live inside a JSON container named by the extension's schema URI, which avoids name clashes. A service provider can define entirely new resource types by publishing a ResourceType and a Schema definition.
sections.eli5: Every card in the box has a few boxes that are always there, like a number tag and a last-changed date. A club can also staple an extra page onto the card for its own questions, and the extra page has its own name so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: The User, Group and Enterprise Schemas
sections.content:
The User schema (urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User) requires one attribute, userName, which must be unique across the provider's Users and is case insensitive. Other singular attributes include name (with formatted, familyName, givenName, middleName, honorificPrefix and honorificSuffix), displayName, nickName, title, userType, preferredLanguage, locale, timezone and active.

Multi-valued attributes are emails, phoneNumbers, ims, photos, addresses, groups, entitlements, roles and x509Certificates. The groups attribute is read-only: membership changes are made through the Group resource.

The password attribute is write-only. Its cleartext or hashed value SHALL NOT be returnable, and a provider that holds it locally SHOULD hash it. It exists to set, replace or compare a password.

The Group schema requires a displayName and has a members list whose values are ids of Users or other Groups, which allows nested groups. The enterprise User extension adds employeeNumber, costCenter, organization, division, department and a manager reference. The RFC defines no authorization model: what group membership allows is left to the service provider.
sections.eli5: The User card has boxes for name, email, phone and a secret word. The Group card is just a name and a list of who is in it. The password box is special: you can write in it, but nobody can ever read it back.

sections.title: Attribute Characteristics
sections.content:
Section 7 defines how a schema describes each attribute. Unless stated otherwise an attribute is not required, has no canonical values, is case insensitive, is readWrite, is returned default, has uniqueness none and is a string.

Mutability says when a value can be set: readOnly (never modified), readWrite (the default), immutable (set at creation or replacement, then never updated) and writeOnly (can be updated but never returned).

Returned says when a value appears in responses: always, never, default or request. Uniqueness is none, server or global. A server MAY reject a value that violates uniqueness with HTTP 400. Other characteristics are caseExact, canonicalValues and, for references, referenceTypes.
sections.eli5: Each box on the form comes with rules: some boxes are locked, some can be filled in once and never changed, and some are secret write-only boxes. The rules are written next to the box so everyone knows them.

sections.title: Describing the Server Itself
sections.content:
Three read-only schemas let a service provider describe itself. The ServiceProviderConfig resource reports which optional features are supported: patch, bulk (with maxOperations and maxPayloadSize), filter (with maxResults), changePassword, sort and etag, plus a list of authenticationSchemes. The RFC defines the scheme type values oauth, oauth2, oauthbearertoken, httpbasic and httpdigest, and says the provider SHOULD make that list publicly accessible so clients can discover how to authenticate.

The ResourceType schema gives a resource type's name, endpoint, base schema URI and optional schema extensions, each flagged as required or not. The Schema schema lists every attribute with its type, sub-attributes, multiplicity and the characteristics above. Schema ids are URIs, so they are portable between providers. Section 8 of the RFC supplies full non-normative JSON examples of all of these.
sections.eli5: A server can hand you a sheet that says what it can do and which forms it uses. You read that sheet first, so you do not guess wrong.

sections.title: Passwords and Privacy
sections.content:
SCIM data is meant to travel over the SCIM protocol, so the security considerations of RFC 7644 also apply. The schema itself raises two concerns.

First, passwords. The protocol uses cleartext passwords for assigning and equality testing, but password values MUST NOT be stored in cleartext form. Administrators SHOULD follow RFC 6819 guidance: validate inputs against injection, store credentials with a protection such as hashing, and where possible avoid passwords as the sole form of authentication.

Second, privacy. All SCIM attributes are treated as sensitive personal information, and attributes such as id, externalId and resource URIs generate new identifying data. The RFC suggests binding identifiers to specific tenants or clients so that separate domains cannot correlate them, limiting access to a need-to-know basis, and sharing only what the other side requires.
sections.eli5: Passwords are like secrets whispered into a locked box, and the box must never be opened in public. All the information about people is private, so share only what is needed.

sections.title: The SCIM URN Namespace and Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:scim and a registry of SCIM schema URIs. URNs have the structure urn:ietf:params:scim:{type}:{name}{:other}, where the type is schemas or api, and the name core is reserved for SCIM specifications.

New core and API schemas MUST be reviewed by a designated expert and published in an RFC. An RFC is also REQUIRED for new data types that modify existing properties and for schema URIs that modify a schema already documented in an RFC. Other URNs under the SCIM prefix MAY be registered with a simple review. Once a name is allocated it MUST NOT be reallocated for a different purpose, so a significant change, such as moving from version 1.0 to 2.0, gets a new registration.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of every extra page anyone has invented, kept by one librarian. Once a name is on the list it can never be given to a different page.
